Let $\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$ be the set of formal real polynomials of
[[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]]. Associate to every
$P\in\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$ an eventually zero coefficient sequence $(p_k)$:
use its displayed finite coefficient list and extend it by zeros when $P\ne0$,
and put $p_k=0$ for every $k$ when $P=0$. Do the same for $Q$, with coefficients
$(q_k)$. Define $P+Q$ coefficientwise and define $PQ$ by the convolution
coefficients
$$ (P+Q)_k=p_k+q_k,\qquad (PQ)_k=\sum_{j=0}^{k}p_jq_{k-j}. $$
using the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. In either construction, discard
trailing zero coefficients; if every coefficient is zero, the result is the zero
polynomial. Scalar multiplication and subtraction are the corresponding
coefficientwise operations. Thus these formulas define operations on the formal
coefficient-list objects, independently of evaluation.

Write $1=(1)$ and $X=(0,1)$, and define
$$ \Phi(P,Q):=(Q,2XQ-P)\qquad(P,Q\in\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}). $$
Apply [[thm-recursion]] to the set
$\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}\times\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$, first with initial value
$(1,X)$ and then with initial value $(1,2X)$, always using the function $\Phi$.
This gives unique pair sequences $H^T,H^U$. Define $T_n$ and $U_n$ to be the
first coordinates of $H^T_n$ and $H^U_n$, respectively. Since the first
coordinate of $\Phi(P,Q)$ is $Q$, the second coordinate of $H^T_n$ is
$T_{n+1}$ and the second coordinate of $H^U_n$ is $U_{n+1}$. Consequently
$$ T_0=1,\quad T_1=X,\quad T_{n+2}=2XT_{n+1}-T_n, $$
$$ U_0=1,\quad U_1=2X,\quad U_{n+2}=2XU_{n+1}-U_n $$
for every $n\in\mathbb N$. These unique sequences are the **Chebyshev
polynomials of the first and second kinds**.

A **formal real polynomial** is either the zero polynomial $0$, or a finite coefficient list $(a_0,\ldots,a_n)$ with $a_n\ne0$; we write the latter as $p(X)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_kX^k$. The list, rather than the function it induces, is the polynomial object. Its **evaluation** at $x\in\mathbb R$ is the real number $p(x):=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_kx^k$.

For nonzero $p=(a_0,\ldots,a_n)$, define $\deg p:=n$ and $\operatorname{lc}(p):=a_n$. The zero polynomial has no degree and no leading coefficient. A nonzero polynomial is **monic** when $\operatorname{lc}(p)=1$. Thus degree and leading coefficient are defined from the displayed finite list, without asserting that distinct formal polynomials define distinct functions. The conventions for finite sums and integer powers used in the evaluation are recorded in [[def-finite-sum]], [[def-integer-power]].

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

Define polynomials $B_m\in\mathbb R[X]$ recursively. Put $B_0(X)=1$. If $m\ge1$ and $B_{m-1}(X)=\sum_{q=0}^{m-1}\beta_{m-1,q}X^q$, set
$$B_m(X):=m\sum_{q=0}^{m-1}\beta_{m-1,q}\left(\frac{X^{q+1}}{q+1}-\frac{1}{(q+1)(q+2)}\right).$$
Natural numbers in real denominators mean their canonical real images from [[def-canonical-natural]]; these images are positive by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and therefore invertible in $\mathbb R$ by [[thm-reals-field]]. Every sum is finite. Write $B_m:=B_m(0)$ for the Bernoulli number of index $m$.

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already

$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading

claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $Q=\prod_{j<n}[a_j,b_j]\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, where $n\ge1$ and every $a_j<b_j$. If $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, then for every permutation of the coordinates the corresponding repeated Riemann integral exists and equals $\int_Qf$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. $f + g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$;
2. for every real $\lambda$, $\lambda f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b \lambda f = \lambda \int_a^b f$;
3. consequently, for all reals $\lambda, \mu$ the function $\lambda f + \mu g$ is
   integrable and
   $$\int_a^b(\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f \;+\; \mu\int_a^b g ;$$
4. the same identity holds with oriented limits: if $u, v \in [a,b]$ and $f, g$
   are integrable between $u$ and $v$ ([[def-oriented-integral]]), then
   $\int_u^v(\lambda f + \mu g) = \lambda\int_u^v f + \mu\int_u^v g$.

**Linearity of the integral is not linearity of the Darboux sums**, and the
proof of claim 1 has to squeeze rather than compute. On a subinterval the
inequality $\sup(f+g) \le \sup f + \sup g$ can be strict — take $f(x) = x$ and
$g(x) = -x$ on $[0,1]$, where the left side is $0$ and the right side is $1$ —
so $U(f+g,P)$ is in general strictly below $U(f,P) + U(g,P)$ and no identity
between upper sums is available. Claim 2, by contrast, is an identity at the
level of the sums, with the roles of $\sup$ and $\inf$ exchanged when
$\lambda < 0$.

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Then:

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]],
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where [[def-oriented-integral]] earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]. Induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ ([[thm-omega-is-peano-system]]) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
([[lem-nat-mult-identity]]) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
([[lem-nat-mult-cancellative]]). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ ([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
([[lem-nat-mult-associative]], [[lem-nat-mult-commutative]]) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional ([[def-nat-multiplication]]), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $E \subseteq [a,b]$ be finite
([[def-countable]], [[def-equinumerous]]), and let $g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$
satisfy

$$g(x) \;=\; f(x) \qquad \text{for every } x \in [a,b] \setminus E .$$

Then $g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and

$$\int_a^b g \;=\; \int_a^b f .$$

In particular the values of an integrand at the endpoints of the interval, and at
any finite set of points, are irrelevant to both questions.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. $|f|$, $f^{2}$ and $fg$ are integrable on $[a,b]$
   ([[def-abs-value]], [[def-integer-power]]);
2. $\max(f,g)$ and $\min(f,g)$, defined pointwise
   ([[def-max-min]]), are integrable on $[a,b]$;
3. the **triangle inequality for the integral**:
   $$\Bigl|\int_a^b f\Bigr| \;\le\; \int_a^b |f| .$$

**Claim 3 is stated with $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** For $u > v$
the right-hand side is $-\int_v^u |f| \le 0$ while the left-hand side is $\ge 0$,
so the inequality as written is false there. The form valid for *every* pair
$u,v$ on which $f$ is integrable ([[def-oriented-integral]]) is

$$\Bigl|\int_u^v f\Bigr| \;\le\; \Bigl|\int_u^v |f|\,\Bigr| ,$$

and that is the form the estimates below on this page use whenever the limits
are not known to be in increasing order.

**The converse of claim 1 fails.** Integrability of $|f|$ does not give
integrability of $f$; the witness is on the companion page.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

derivations.claim: We first establish Taylor's integral remainder by induction on the natural order $q$ ([[thm-induction-principle]]). For $r=1$, [F3] gives $f(x)=f(a)+\int_a^xf'(t)\,dt$. If the remainder formula holds at order $q\ge1$, put $u(t):=(x-t)^q/q!$. The product rule and FTC give $\int_a^xu'(t)f^{(q)}(t)\,dt=[u(t)f^{(q)}(t)]_a^x-\int_a^xu(t)f^{(q+1)}(t)\,dt$, and $u'(t)=-(x-t)^{q-1}/(q-1)!$. Rearranging yields $\int_a^x\frac{(x-t)^{q-1}}{(q-1)!}f^{(q)}(t)\,dt=\frac{(x-a)^q}{q!}f^{(q)}(a)+\int_a^x\frac{(x-t)^q}{q!}f^{(q+1)}(t)\,dt.$ Thus induction yields $f(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}f^{(j)}(a)(x-a)^j/j!+\int_a^x(x-t)^{r-1}f^{(r)}(t)/(r-1)!\,dt$.

Extend the last integral to $[a,b]$ by setting its kernel to zero when $t\ge x$. With $P_{r-1}(x):=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}f^{(j)}(a)(x-a)^j/j!$, the result is $f(x)=P_{r-1}(x)+\int_a^bg_{r,t}(x)f^{(r)}(t)\,dt$. Since $Q$ is exact on $\mathcal P_{r-1}$, $L(P_{r-1})=0$.

Suppose first that $r\ge2$. The function $(x,t)\mapsto g_{r,t}(x)f^{(r)}(t)$ is continuous on $[a,b]^2$ because $r-1\ge1$ and $f^{(r)}$ is continuous. By [F5]–[F7], applying the integral part of $L$ to step 2.1 and interchanging the two rectangle integrals gives $\int_a^b(\int_a^bg_{r,t}(x)\,dx)f^{(r)}(t)\,dt$. Each finite evaluation term of $Q$ commutes with the $t$-integral by [F6]. Therefore $L(f)=\int_a^bL(g_{r,t})f^{(r)}(t)\,dt=\int_a^bK_r(t)f^{(r)}(t)\,dt$. The function $(x,t)\mapsto g_{r,t}(x)$ is uniformly continuous on the compact square by [F8], so its $x$-integral and its finite weighted evaluations vary continuously with $t$; hence $K_r$ is continuous and integrable.

If $r=1$, exactness on constants gives $\sum_iw_i=b-a$. For $t$ outside the finite node set, [F1] gives $K_1(t)=(b-t)-\sum_{x_i>t}w_i$. It is bounded and affine between consecutive nodes. Extend each affine piece continuously to its closed subinterval; the resulting pieces are integrable by [F7] and add to an integrable piecewise function by [F6]. The kernel differs from that function at only finitely many nodes, so it is integrable and has the same integral by [F9]. Since $f'$ is continuous, [F10] makes $K_1f'$ integrable; changing the kernel values at the finite node set does not change that product integral by [F9]. By [F3]–[F4] and integration by parts, $\int_a^b(b-t)f'(t)\,dt=\int_a^bf(t)\,dt-(b-a)f(a)$, while $\sum_iw_i\int_a^{x_i}f'(t)\,dt=Q(f)-(b-a)f(a)$. Subtracting gives $\int_a^bK_1(t)f'(t)\,dt=L(f)$.

By [F2] and [F11], $f^{(r)}$ is bounded on $[a,b]$, so $\|f^{(r)}\|_\infty<\infty$. In either case, the kernel is integrable and $|K_r|$ is integrable by [F10]. Apply monotonicity in [F10] to $-|K_r|\|f^{(r)}\|_\infty\le K_r f^{(r)}\le |K_r|\|f^{(r)}\|_\infty$, and use the representation in step 3.1 or 3.2. This gives the asserted bound.

Let $a<b$ be real numbers, let $N\ge1$ be an integer, put
$h:=(b-a)/N$, and let $x_j:=a+jh$ for $0\le j\le N$. For any real-valued
function $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, its **composite trapezoidal value** with $N$
equal panels is
$$T_N(f):=h\left(\frac{f(x_0)}2+\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}f(x_j)+\frac{f(x_N)}2\right).$$
The sum is the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]; when $N=1$ it is empty and
equals $0$. This definition gives a finite real number for every such $f$.
An error comparison with $\int_a^b f$ is asserted only when that integral is
defined.

Define polynomials $B_m\in\mathbb R[X]$ recursively. Put $B_0(X)=1$. If $m\ge1$ and $B_{m-1}(X)=\sum_{q=0}^{m-1}\beta_{m-1,q}X^q$, set
$$B_m(X):=m\sum_{q=0}^{m-1}\beta_{m-1,q}\left(\frac{X^{q+1}}{q+1}-\frac{1}{(q+1)(q+2)}\right).$$
Natural numbers in real denominators mean their canonical real images from [[def-canonical-natural]]; these images are positive by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and therefore invertible in $\mathbb R$ by [[thm-reals-field]]. Every sum is finite. Write $B_m:=B_m(0)$ for the Bernoulli number of index $m$.

For the polynomials of [[def-na-bernoulli-polynomials]] and every integer $m\ge1$,
$$B'_m(x)=mB_{m-1}(x),\qquad \int_0^1 B_m(x)\,dx=0.$$
In particular, $B_0(x)=1$ and $B_1(x)=x-\tfrac12$.
Consequently $B_m(1)=B_m(0)$ for $m\ge2$. The reflection identity $B_m(1-x)=(-1)^mB_m(x)$ holds for every $m\ge0$, so $B_m(0)=0$ for odd $m\ge3$. Each $B_m$ is bounded on $[0,1]$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and $f:I\to\mathbb R$. Put $f^{(0)}:=f$. Recursively, wherever $f^{(j)}$ is differentiable, put $f^{(j+1)}:=(f^{(j)})'$, with derivatives at endpoints understood in the one-sided sense fixed by [[def-derivative]] and [[def-one-sided-limits]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, the function is **$k$-times differentiable** on $I$ if $f^{(j)}$ exists on $I$ for every $j\le k$. It is of class **$C^k$** on $I$ if these derivatives exist and every $f^{(j)}$, $0\le j\le k$, is continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). It is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, if it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Since $0\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), $C^0$ means continuity. The definitions also give $C^{k+1}\subseteq C^k$. Existence of $f^{(k)}$ alone does not assert that $f^{(k)}$ is continuous.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. $f + g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$;
2. for every real $\lambda$, $\lambda f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b \lambda f = \lambda \int_a^b f$;
3. consequently, for all reals $\lambda, \mu$ the function $\lambda f + \mu g$ is
   integrable and
   $$\int_a^b(\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f \;+\; \mu\int_a^b g ;$$
4. the same identity holds with oriented limits: if $u, v \in [a,b]$ and $f, g$
   are integrable between $u$ and $v$ ([[def-oriented-integral]]), then
   $\int_u^v(\lambda f + \mu g) = \lambda\int_u^v f + \mu\int_u^v g$.

**Linearity of the integral is not linearity of the Darboux sums**, and the
proof of claim 1 has to squeeze rather than compute. On a subinterval the
inequality $\sup(f+g) \le \sup f + \sup g$ can be strict — take $f(x) = x$ and
$g(x) = -x$ on $[0,1]$, where the left side is $0$ and the right side is $1$ —
so $U(f+g,P)$ is in general strictly below $U(f,P) + U(g,P)$ and no identity
between upper sums is available. Claim 2, by contrast, is an identity at the
level of the sums, with the roles of $\sup$ and $\inf$ exchanged when
$\lambda < 0$.

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Then:

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]],
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where [[def-oriented-integral]] earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]. Induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ ([[thm-omega-is-peano-system]]) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
([[lem-nat-mult-identity]]) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
([[lem-nat-mult-cancellative]]). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ ([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
([[lem-nat-mult-associative]], [[lem-nat-mult-commutative]]) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional ([[def-nat-multiplication]]), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

derivations.claim: On a panel $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$, put $u=(x-x_i)/h$. Integration by parts using $B_1(u)=u-\tfrac12$ gives $h\int_{x_i}^{x_{i+1}}B_1(u)f'(x)\,dx=\frac h2\bigl(f(x_i)+f(x_{i+1})\bigr)-\int_{x_i}^{x_{i+1}}f(x)\,dx.$ Summing this identity over the $N$ panels and using [F1] and [F5] yields $T_N(f)-\int_a^b f=J_1$, where $J_k:=\frac{h^k}{k!}\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\int_{x_i}^{x_{i+1}}B_k(u_i(x))f^{(k)}(x)\,dx$ for $1\le k\le2p$.

For $1\le k<2p$, differentiate $B_{k+1}(u_i(x))$ to get $(k+1)B_k(u_i(x))/h$. Integrating by parts on each panel therefore gives $J_k=\frac{h^{k+1}}{(k+1)!}\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\bigl[B_{k+1}(u_i(x))f^{(k)}(x)\bigr]_{x_i}^{x_{i+1}}-J_{k+1}.$ Because $B_{k+1}(1)=B_{k+1}(0)$ by [F2], the interior endpoint terms telescope, leaving $\frac{h^{k+1}B_{k+1}}{(k+1)!}(f^{(k)}(b)-f^{(k)}(a))$ as the boundary term.

Write $b_q:=\frac{B_qh^q}{q!}(f^{(q-1)}(b)-f^{(q-1)}(a))$ for $q\ge2$. If $k+1$ is odd and at least $3$, [F2] makes that boundary term zero, so step 1.2 gives $J_k=-J_{k+1}$. If $k+1=2r$ is even, step 1.2 gives $J_{2r-1}=b_{2r}-J_{2r}$. For each $r<p$, the odd-index recurrence at $k=2r$ gives $J_{2r}=-J_{2r+1}$; hence $J_{2r-1}=b_{2r}+J_{2r+1}$. Finite induction on $r=1,\ldots,p-1$ ([[thm-induction-principle]]) iterates these identities; followed by the final even-index recurrence, it gives $J_1=\sum_{r=1}^{p}\frac{B_{2r}h^{2r}}{(2r)!}\bigl(f^{(2r-1)}(b)-f^{(2r-1)}(a)\bigr)-J_{2p}.$

The polynomial $B_{2p}$ is continuous by [F2], so [F7] ensures $M_{2p}=\max_{[0,1]}|B_{2p}|$ exists and is finite. By the definition of $J_{2p}$ and the bound $|B_{2p}(u)|\le M_{2p}$ on each unit cell, $|J_{2p}|\le h^{2p}M_{2p}\|f^{(2p)}\|_\infty\sum_i(x_{i+1}-x_i)/(2p)!=(b-a)M_{2p}h^{2p}\|f^{(2p)}\|_\infty/(2p)!$. Substituting step 2.1 into step 1.1 proves the stated formula and remainder bound.

Let $a<b$, let $N\ge1$ and $p\ge1$ be integers, put $h=(b-a)/N$ and $x_i=a+ih$, and let $f\in C^{2p}([a,b])$ in the sense of [[def-higher-derivatives-and-smoothness]]. Write $B_m(x)$ for [[def-na-bernoulli-polynomials]] and $B_m:=B_m(0)$. For $u_i(x):=(x-x_i)/h$ on $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$, the composite trapezoidal value $T_N(f)$ of [[def-composite-trapezoidal-rule]] satisfies
$$T_N(f)=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx+\sum_{r=1}^{p}\frac{B_{2r}h^{2r}}{(2r)!}\bigl(f^{(2r-1)}(b)-f^{(2r-1)}(a)\bigr)-\frac{h^{2p}}{(2p)!}\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\int_{x_i}^{x_{i+1}}B_{2p}(u_i(x))f^{(2p)}(x)\,dx.$$
In particular, with $M_{2p}:=\max_{0\le u\le1}|B_{2p}(u)|$, the absolute value of the final remainder is at most $(b-a)M_{2p}h^{2p}\|f^{(2p)}\|_\infty/(2p)!$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and $f:I\to\mathbb R$. Put $f^{(0)}:=f$. Recursively, wherever $f^{(j)}$ is differentiable, put $f^{(j+1)}:=(f^{(j)})'$, with derivatives at endpoints understood in the one-sided sense fixed by [[def-derivative]] and [[def-one-sided-limits]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, the function is **$k$-times differentiable** on $I$ if $f^{(j)}$ exists on $I$ for every $j\le k$. It is of class **$C^k$** on $I$ if these derivatives exist and every $f^{(j)}$, $0\le j\le k$, is continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). It is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, if it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Since $0\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), $C^0$ means continuity. The definitions also give $C^{k+1}\subseteq C^k$. Existence of $f^{(k)}$ alone does not assert that $f^{(k)}$ is continuous.

Let $a<b$ be real numbers, let $N\ge1$ be an integer, put
$h:=(b-a)/N$, and let $x_j:=a+jh$ for $0\le j\le N$. For any real-valued
function $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, its **composite trapezoidal value** with $N$
equal panels is
$$T_N(f):=h\left(\frac{f(x_0)}2+\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}f(x_j)+\frac{f(x_N)}2\right).$$
The sum is the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]; when $N=1$ it is empty and
equals $0$. This definition gives a finite real number for every such $f$.
An error comparison with $\int_a^b f$ is asserted only when that integral is
defined.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.

$$w_j:=\frac{1}{14175}(989,5888,-928,10496,-4540,10496,-928,5888,989)_j.$$

$$Q_8(f):=\sum_{j=0}^{8}w_j f(x_j),$$
where the sum is finite. The nodes are equally spaced and include both endpoints; the subsequent weight and exactness lemma verifies that these coefficients are the integrated Lagrange-cardinal weights.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge0$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be distinct real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$. Define the node polynomial and barycentric weights by
$$\omega_n(X)=\prod_{k=0}^{n}(X-x_k),\qquad w_j=\left(\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le n\\k\ne j}}(x_j-x_k)\right)^{-1}\quad(0\le j\le n).$$
An empty product is $1$, so $w_0=1$ when $n=0$.

In these formulas, $X$ is a real argument, and for real $a$ and nonzero real $b$, $a/b$ denotes $ab^{-1}$ in the field $\mathbb R$ ([[def-field]]).

For each $j$, the cardinal function is
$$\ell_j(X)=\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le n\\k\ne j}}\frac{X-x_k}{x_j-x_k}.$$

Strict ordering gives $x_j-\widehat x_{j,k}\ne0$ for every factor, so [[lem-finite-product-of-nonzero-reals-is-nonzero]] and the field inverse law make each $w_j$ well defined.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$. Each cardinal function $\ell_j$ of [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]] is the evaluation of a formal polynomial of degree $n$. The node function $\omega_n$ is the evaluation of a monic formal polynomial of degree $n+1$, and $\omega_n(x)\ne0$ whenever $x$ differs from every node. Let $\phi:[c,d]\to[a,b]$ be a monotone surjection, differentiable on $[c,d]$ in the one-sided endpoint sense, with Riemann-integrable derivative. For every bounded $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$,
$$f\text{ is Riemann integrable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(f\circ\phi)|\phi'|\text{ is Riemann integrable},$$
and, when these conditions hold,
$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=\int_c^d f(\phi(t))|\phi'(t)|\,dt.$$
Flat subintervals of $\phi$ are allowed.

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. $f + g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$;
2. for every real $\lambda$, $\lambda f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b \lambda f = \lambda \int_a^b f$;
3. consequently, for all reals $\lambda, \mu$ the function $\lambda f + \mu g$ is
   integrable and
   $$\int_a^b(\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f \;+\; \mu\int_a^b g ;$$
4. the same identity holds with oriented limits: if $u, v \in [a,b]$ and $f, g$
   are integrable between $u$ and $v$ ([[def-oriented-integral]]), then
   $\int_u^v(\lambda f + \mu g) = \lambda\int_u^v f + \mu\int_u^v g$.

**Linearity of the integral is not linearity of the Darboux sums**, and the
proof of claim 1 has to squeeze rather than compute. On a subinterval the
inequality $\sup(f+g) \le \sup f + \sup g$ can be strict — take $f(x) = x$ and
$g(x) = -x$ on $[0,1]$, where the left side is $0$ and the right side is $1$ —

between upper sums is available. Claim 2, by contrast, is an identity at the
level of the sums, with the roles of $\sup$ and $\inf$ exchanged when
$\lambda < 0$.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$ and let $y=(y_0,\ldots,y_n)\in\mathbb R^{n+1}$. In real-valued formulas, each natural index denotes its canonical real image ([[def-canonical-natural]]). Since $n>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]], division by $n$ is defined in $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-reals-field]]). The type-I discrete cosine transform, in the Lobatto convention used here, is the vector $X=(X_0,\ldots,X_n)$ defined by
$$X_k:=y_0+(-1)^k y_n+2\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}y_j\cos\!\left(\frac{j k\pi}{n}\right),\qquad 0\le k\le n.$$
Here $(-1)^k$ is the natural power of the real number $-1$ from [[def-integer-power]], and the sum is the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]], empty when $n=1$. The data $y_j$ are ordered from the right endpoint toward the left endpoint at nodes $\cos(j\pi/n)$. This definition fixes the unnormalised DCT-I convention; the transform is not defined at $n=0$.

For $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$ and $k,\ell\in\mathbb N$ with $0\le k,\ell\le n$, define
$$S_{k\ell}:=\frac12\cos(0)+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\cos\!\left(\frac{j k\pi}{n}\right)\cos\!\left(\frac{j \ell\pi}{n}\right)+\frac12(-1)^{k+\ell}.$$
Then $S_{k\ell}=n$ when $k=\ell=0$ or $k=\ell=n$, $S_{k\ell}=n/2$ when $k=\ell$ is strictly between $0$ and $n$, and $S_{k\ell}=0$ when $k\ne\ell$. The half-endpoint convention is the one used by the DCT-I of [[def-na-clenshaw-curtis-dct-i]].

For every integer $n\ge0$ and every real $\theta$, the first-kind Chebyshev polynomial from [[def-chebyshev-polynomials-first-and-second-kind]] satisfies
$$T_n(\cos\theta)=\cos(n\theta).$$

Let $C[-1,1]$ be the real continuous functions on $[-1,1]$, with
$\|f\|_\infty:=\sup_{x\in[-1,1]}|f(x)|$. Let $\mathcal P_n$ be the
restrictions to $[-1,1]$ of real polynomials of degree at most $n$, including
the zero polynomial. Interval notation is that of [[def-interval]]. Continuity and polynomial degree have the conventions of
[[def-continuity-real]] and
[[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]].

For each $n\in\mathbb N$ (with naturals in real expressions interpreted by
their canonical real images), the first-kind Chebyshev root angles and nodes are
$$\theta_j^{R,n}=\frac{(2j+1)\pi}{2n+2},\qquad x_j^{R,n}=\cos\theta_j^{R,n},\qquad 0\leq j\leq n.$$
They are the roots of $T_{n+1}$ by
[[thm-chebyshev-multiple-angle-identities]]. For $n\geq1$, the
Chebyshev–Lobatto angles and nodes are
$$\theta_j^{L,n}=\frac{j\pi}{n},\qquad x_j^{L,n}=\cos\theta_j^{L,n},\qquad 0\leq j\leq n.$$
They include both endpoints and are the extrema of $T_n$ by the same
identity. At $n=0$, define the Lobatto node to be $x_0^{L,0}=0$. The
cosine is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$, so each listed family has
distinct nodes; the root family at $n=0$ also consists of $0$.

For either family $\sigma\in\{R,L\}$, write its nodes as
$x_0,\ldots,x_n$ and define
$$\ell_{j,n}^{\sigma}(x)= \prod_{\substack{0\leq k\leq n\\k\ne j}} \frac{x-x_k}{x_j-x_k},\qquad I_n^\sigma f=\sum_{j=0}^n f(x_j)\ell_{j,n}^{\sigma}.$$
These are the cardinal formula and interpolation sum of
[[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]] specialized to this node family.
The displayed cosine arrays decrease, whereas that supplier orders nodes
increasingly: use $z_i=x_{n-i}$ and data $y_i=f(z_i)$. Its cardinal
function with index $n-j$ is exactly the displayed $\ell_{j,n}^\sigma$,
by reindexing the finite product, and its interpolation sum is $I_n^\sigma$.
The empty product at $n=0$ is $1$, so the same identification holds for the
single node. Distinctness makes every denominator nonzero;
[[lem-cardinal-basis-degree-and-values]] supplies the degree and cardinal
values. The finite sum is linear in the data and maps $C[-1,1]$ into
$\mathcal P_n$. Its operator norm is
$$\Lambda_n^\sigma:= \sup\{\|I_n^\sigma g\|_\infty:g\in C[-1,1],\ \|g\|_\infty\leq1\}.$$
If $\ell_{j,n}^\sigma(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n a_{jk}x^k$, then
$|\ell_{j,n}^\sigma(x)|\leq\sum_{k=0}^n|a_{jk}|$ for $|x|\leq1$; hence
$\|I_n^\sigma g\|_\infty\leq\sum_{j,k}|a_{jk}|<\infty$ whenever
$\|g\|_\infty\leq1$. Define the best degree-$n$ uniform
approximation error by
$$E_n(f):=\inf_{p\in\mathcal P_n}\|f-p\|_\infty .$$

Natural powers in real scalar expressions are understood through their canonical real images.
2. For $j=1,\ldots,L$, and then for each $\ell=j,\ldots,L$, set
$$R_{\ell,j}:=R_{\ell,j-1}+\frac{R_{\ell,j-1}-R_{\ell-1,j-1}}{4^j-1}.$$

For $j\ge1$, claim 3 of [[lem-power-monotone]] gives $4^j\ge4>1$, using the natural-to-real power identity of [[def-nat-power]]; thus every displayed denominator $4^j-1$ is the positive real $4^j-1$ and is invertible by [[thm-reals-field]]. This definition returns only the stated finite table; it makes no accuracy claim for nonsmooth inputs or finite-precision arithmetic.

Let $a<b$, let $j\ge1$ be an integer, and let $f\in C^{2j+2}([a,b])$. For $N\ge1$ set $h=(b-a)/N$, $I=\int_a^b f$, and
$$c_r:=\frac{B_{2r}}{(2r)!}\bigl(f^{(2r-1)}(b)-f^{(2r-1)}(a)\bigr),\qquad 1\le r\le j+1,$$
using the Bernoulli numbers of [[def-na-bernoulli-polynomials]]. Then
$$T_N(f)=I+\sum_{r=1}^{j}c_rh^{2r}+\varepsilon_N,\qquad |\varepsilon_N|\le C_jh^{2j+2},$$
where the level-independent finite constant
$$C_j:=|c_{j+1}|+\frac{(b-a)M_{2j+2}}{(2j+2)!}\|f^{(2j+2)}\|_\infty,\qquad M_{2j+2}:=\max_{0\le u\le1}|B_{2j+2}(u)|,$$
does not depend on $N$. Thus the remainder bound is uniform over every set of dyadic levels.

derivations.claim: By [F1]–[F2], column zero has the expansion $R_{\ell,0}=I+\sum_{r=1}^m c_rh_\ell^{2r}+\varepsilon_{\ell,0}$ uniformly for $\ell\ge0$. We prove by induction on the column $j$ that, for every $\ell\ge j$, $R_{\ell,j}=I+\sum_{r=j+1}^{m}d_{r,j}h_\ell^{2r}+\varepsilon_{\ell,j},\qquad |\varepsilon_{\ell,j}|\le C_jh_\ell^{2m+2},$ with coefficients $d_{r,j}$ independent of $\ell$. For $j=0$, this is [F2] with $d_{r,0}=c_r$.

Assume the induction hypothesis for column $j-1$ with $1\le j\le m$. Then $R_{\ell,j-1}$ has terms indexed $r=j,\ldots,m$ and $R_{\ell-1,j-1}$ has the same coefficients with $h_{\ell-1}^{2r}=4^rh_\ell^{2r}$ by [F3]. Substitution in [F1] multiplies the coefficient of $h_\ell^{2r}$ by $1+\frac{1-4^r}{4^j-1}=\frac{4^j-4^r}{4^j-1}.$ For $r=j$ this factor is zero, so the $j$th error power cancels; the remaining powers have indices $r>j$.

The new remainder is $\varepsilon_{\ell,j}=\varepsilon_{\ell,j-1}+(\varepsilon_{\ell,j-1}-\varepsilon_{\ell-1,j-1})/(4^j-1)$. Thus $|\varepsilon_{\ell,j}|\le C_{j-1}\left(1+\frac{1+2^{2m+2}}{4^j-1}\right)h_\ell^{2m+2},$ so a finite level-independent $C_j$ exists under the inductive remainder bound.

Step 1.1 supplies the base column, and steps 2.1 and 3.1 advance the expansion and its uniform remainder from column $j-1$ to column $j$. By [F4], induction therefore gives the asserted expansion at every column through $m$. At $j=m$ the coefficient sum is empty, so $R_{L,m}=I+\varepsilon_{L,m}$, and step 3.1 bounds its remainder by $C_mh_L^{2m+2}$.

With the Chebyshev moments $\mu_k$ of [[lem-na-chebyshev-integral-moments]], define
$$Q_{n,[a,b]}(f):=d\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_k\mu_k.$$
For $n=0$, define instead
$$Q_{0,[a,b]}(f):=(b-a)f(m),$$
the midpoint rule. This is the explicit endpoint and zero-degree convention for Clenshaw–Curtis quadrature. The sums and coefficients are exact real quantities; finite-precision evaluation is a separate algorithm.

$$a_0:=\frac{X_0}{2n},\qquad a_n:=\frac{X_n}{2n},\qquad a_k:=\frac{X_k}{n}\quad(1\le k<n).$$

For every integer $k\ge0$, let $\mu_k:=\int_{-1}^{1}T_k(x)\,dx$, where $T_k$ is the first-kind Chebyshev polynomial. Then
$$\mu_k=\begin{cases}2,&k=0,\\0,&k\text{ odd},\\[2pt]\dfrac{2}{1-k^2},&k\ge2\text{ even}.\end{cases}$$
Equivalently, $\mu_{2r}=2/(1-4r^2)$ for every integer $r\ge0$.

polynomials in [[def-best-uniform-polynomial-approximation-error-and-chebyshev-interpolants]]
satisfy $\ell_{j,n}^{\sigma}(x_k^{\sigma,n})=1$ when $j=k$ and $0$
otherwise. They are the unique degree-at-most-$n$ polynomials with those
cardinal values. Consequently $I_n^\sigma p=p$ for every $p\in\mathcal P_n$.
Moreover,
$$\Lambda_n^\sigma= \sup_{x\in[-1,1]}\sum_{j=0}^n|\ell_{j,n}^{\sigma}(x)|.$$

For either Chebyshev node family, every $n\geq0$, and every

Here $E_n$ is the best degree-$n$ uniform error and $\Lambda_n^\sigma$
is the operator norm defined in

continuous, and sums and scalar multiples of continuous functions remain
continuous by [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]. The interval
$[-1,1]\subset\mathbb R$ is nonempty, closed, and bounded, so
[[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]] implies

maximum values $m_h,M_h$. Since $m_h\leq h(x)\leq M_h$, one has

therefore gives the stated finite supremum and infimum. Also, $n+1$ has
positive real image by [[def-canonical-natural]] and

range are nonzero.

A **formal real polynomial** is either the zero polynomial $0$, or a finite coefficient list $(a_0,\ldots,a_n)$ with $a_n\ne0$; we write the latter as $p(X)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_kX^k$. The list, rather than the function it induces, is the polynomial object. Its **evaluation** at $x\in\mathbb R$ is the real number $p(x):=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_kx^k$.

For nonzero $p=(a_0,\ldots,a_n)$, define $\deg p:=n$ and $\operatorname{lc}(p):=a_n$. The zero polynomial has no degree and no leading coefficient. A nonzero polynomial is **monic** when $\operatorname{lc}(p)=1$. Thus degree and leading coefficient are defined from the displayed finite list, without asserting that distinct formal polynomials define distinct functions. The conventions for finite sums and integer powers used in the evaluation are recorded in [[def-finite-sum]], [[def-integer-power]].

For all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$,

$$(x+y)^{n} \;=\; \sum_{k<n+1} \iota\binom{n}{k}\, x^{k}\, y^{\,n-k},$$

where the powers are the integer powers of [[def-integer-power]], the sum is the
real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] over $k = 0, 1, \dots, n$, the difference
$n-k$ is a genuine one because $k \le n$ throughout the range, and $\iota$ is the
canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]].

**The coefficient is $\iota\binom{n}{k}$ and not $\binom{n}{k}$.** A binomial
coefficient is a natural number, that is a von Neumann natural, that is a set; it
is not an element of $\mathbb{R}$, and it enters the field through $\iota$.

**The identity is stated in $\mathbb{R}$ and only in $\mathbb{R}$.** The same
proof uses nothing but commutativity, associativity, distributivity and
natural-number multiples of a ring element, so a commutative-ring version is
available wherever rings are; rings are not available at this point in the
reading order, and the ring statement is a separate statement, to be made where
they are. See the Remarks below.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $\phi:[c,d]\to[a,b]$ be a monotone surjection, differentiable on $[c,d]$ in the one-sided endpoint sense, with Riemann-integrable derivative. For every bounded $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$,
$$f\text{ is Riemann integrable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(f\circ\phi)|\phi'|\text{ is Riemann integrable},$$
and, when these conditions hold,
$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=\int_c^d f(\phi(t))|\phi'(t)|\,dt.$$
Flat subintervals of $\phi$ are allowed.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. $f + g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$;
2. for every real $\lambda$, $\lambda f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b \lambda f = \lambda \int_a^b f$;
3. consequently, for all reals $\lambda, \mu$ the function $\lambda f + \mu g$ is
   integrable and
   $$\int_a^b(\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f \;+\; \mu\int_a^b g ;$$
4. the same identity holds with oriented limits: if $u, v \in [a,b]$ and $f, g$
   are integrable between $u$ and $v$ ([[def-oriented-integral]]), then
   $\int_u^v(\lambda f + \mu g) = \lambda\int_u^v f + \mu\int_u^v g$.

**Linearity of the integral is not linearity of the Darboux sums**, and the
proof of claim 1 has to squeeze rather than compute. On a subinterval the
inequality $\sup(f+g) \le \sup f + \sup g$ can be strict — take $f(x) = x$ and
$g(x) = -x$ on $[0,1]$, where the left side is $0$ and the right side is $1$ —
so $U(f+g,P)$ is in general strictly below $U(f,P) + U(g,P)$ and no identity
between upper sums is available. Claim 2, by contrast, is an identity at the
level of the sums, with the roles of $\sup$ and $\inf$ exchanged when
$\lambda < 0$.

derivations.claim: For $n\ge1$, let $p_n(t)=\sum_{k=0}^na_kT_k(t)$. By [F1]–[F3] and [F10], $Q_{n,[a,b]}(f)=d\sum_k a_k\int_{-1}^1T_k(t)\,dt=d\int_{-1}^1p_n(t)\,dt$. The affine substitution [F9] makes this $\int_a^bP(x)\,dx$ for $P(x)=p_n((x-m)/d)$, and [F2] identifies $P$ with the interpolant pullback. For $n=0$, [F1] is the integral of the constant polynomial $P(x)=f(m)$ by [F9]. Thus $Q_{n,[a,b]}(f)=\int_a^bP(x)\,dx$ in every case.

Let $q$ be any polynomial of degree at most $n$ on $[a,b]$ and put $\tilde q(t)=q(m+dt)$. By [F7], $\tilde q\in\mathcal P_n$. The interpolation reproduction in [F4] gives $I_n^L\tilde q=\tilde q$, so step 1.1 yields $Q_{n,[a,b]}(q)=\int_a^bq(x)\,dx$. This proves polynomial exactness.

Set $P(x)=I_n^L g((x-m)/d)$ as in step 1.1. The pullback bijection gives $\|f-P\|_{\infty,[a,b]}=\|g-I_n^L g\|_{\infty,[-1,1]}$. By [F8], $|\int_a^b(f-P)|\le(b-a)\|f-P\|_\infty$. Combining this with $Q(f)=\int P$ from step 1.1 and [F5] proves the displayed bound.

For each $p\in\mathcal P_n$ on $[-1,1]$, the pullback $x\mapsto p((x-m)/d)$ is in $\mathcal P_n$ on $[a,b]$ by [F7] and has the same supremum error against $f$ as $p$ has against $g$. Conversely, every degree-at-most-$n$ polynomial on $[a,b]$ pulls back to one on $[-1,1]$. The two infima defining best uniform error are therefore equal.
